title: Ingress surge tempering lab notes
content:
Purpose:
- Quick personal log of an experiment exploring a lightweight "tempering" strategy for sudden ingress surges hitting pooled GPU backends. Goal is to reduce p99 tail amplification during short bursts (10s-60s) while preserving median latency and overall QPS.

Context / motivation:
- Observed customer behavior: sudden cold-start-like bursts at scale (ad-hoc batch sends from downstream aggregator) cause p99 to spike 2.5–3x for 30-90s windows even when average QPS is well within capacity.
- Hypothesis: transient queue formation + interactive KV cache misses + monolithic batch sizing produce elongated tails. A thin, reversible admission control ("tempering") that smooths ingress for short windows may keep real p99 low without large throughput loss.

Test plan (short):
1) Compare baseline (direct routing, fixed batch-size 32, no prefetch) vs. tempering (token-prefetch hint + soft admission control) on same pod pool.
2) Use synthetic client arrivals that mimic real spike: base 150 qps, then 900 qps for 30s, then back to 150 qps. Repeated 6 cycles over 20 minutes.
3) Run across two hardware configs: A100-80GB cluster (8 pods) and mixed T4 pool (16 pods). Model: rwd-mini-7b-quant (int8 fallback path).
4) Measure p50/p95/p99, 99.9, mean latency, successful tokens/s, KV-cache hit-rate, and effective batch size distribution. Track error/fallback rates.

Commands and harness:
- Client driver: custom runner harness (bench/harness/ingress-temper) with arrival profile JSON.
- Example invocation: 
  ./bench/harness --profile profiles/zipf-bursts-150-900-30s.json --target http://loadbalancer:8080/generate --concurrency 256 --duration 1200 --out results/ingress-temper-a100-20251102.json
- Server config (baseline): batch_size: 32, max_latency_ms: 80, prefetch: false, admit: none.
- Server config (tempering): batch_size: 32, soft_admit_window_ms: 1000, prefetch_hint_tokens: 8, admission_penalty_factor: 0.6 (probabilistic accept throttle)

Key observations (A100 run):
- Baseline:
  p50: 22ms, p95: 48ms, p99: 220ms, p999: 520ms.
  mean latency: 46ms, throughput (tokens/s): 42k.
  batch size distribution during spike: 24-32 heavy (average 29). KV-cache hit-rate dropped from 87% to 63% during first 10s of spike.
  Notes: p99 dominated by a subset of requests that saw both large batch queuing delays and cold KV misses.
- Tempering:
  p50: 24ms, p95: 51ms, p99: 95ms, p999: 210ms.
  mean latency: 44ms, throughput (tokens/s): 39.8k (5% drop).
  batch size distribution: more small batches (12-28) during ramp-up; admission reduced instantaneous queue depth. KV-cache hit-rate stayed higher (80% -> 76% during spike).
  Notes: p99 improved massively (220->95ms). Some customers sounding notes: slight visible increase in median but much better tail.

Key observations (T4 pool):
- Baseline:
  p50: 38ms, p95: 110ms, p99: 520ms, p999: 1.4s.
  mean latency 130ms, tokens/s: 18k. KV hit-rate 74%->50% at peak.
- Tempering:
  p50: 40ms, p95: 120ms, p99: 260ms, p999: 720ms.
  mean latency 120ms, tokens/s: 17k (6% drop). KV hit-rate: 68%->60% at peak.

Takeaways (quick):
- Tempering (soft admission + small prefetch hints) traded ~5-6% throughput for ~55-60% reduction in p99 on A100 and ~50% reduction on T4. p50 impact minimal.
- Much of p99 improvement linked to preserving KV-cache hit rate (avoiding large simultaneous cache churn) and preventing queue spikes that allow very large batches to accumulate.
- Admission penalty factor tuning matters: aggressive admission (0.3) saved more tail but dropped throughput >12% and raised p50 noticeably. 0.6 looked like good middle ground.

Behavioral notes / anomalies:
- First cycle warm-up: A100 baseline exhibited a cascade where first 8s of spike cause massive cache churn; later cycles less severe (cache warmed). Tempering stabilized first cycle too.
- Observed a small increase in duplicate requests from client-side retry logic when tempering introduced 503s at high aggressiveness—harmful if upstream retries are not backoff-aware.
- Under mixed-tenant load (simulated low-priority background jobs), tempering still improves tail but throughput hit is higher (8-10%) — likely because background jobs soak small-batch slack.

Quick follow-ups / TODOs:
- Run tempering + adaptive batch sizing (reduce max batch during detected spike windows) combo to see if we can recover throughput while keeping p99 low.
- Try prefetch_hint_tokens tuned per model length (8 was arbitrary). Evaluate cost of wasted tokens vs cache benefits.
- Add backoff-aware signals to ingress proxy so client retries don't amplify 503s (PR linked above).
- Validate with real customer traffic replay (anonymized) to ensure behavior matches synthetic pattern.
- Instrument admission decisions in tracing so we can compute fraction of requests admitted vs delayed for postmortems.

Quick verdict for shipping pilot:
- Tempering is promising as an opt-in SLO-preserving feature for bursty tenants. Recommend pilot behind a feature flag for select customers (opt-in), release UI knobs in console (soft_admit_window, admission_penalty).

Notes to self (short):
- Keep aggression conservative by default. Add telemetry for retry amplification.
- Communicate expected throughput delta (~5–8%) when marketing feature.
- Add tests in bench harness for mixed-tenant to capture worst-case throughput drop.

Raw numbers (selected time slice snapshot, A100, cycle 2, seconds 12-22):
- Ingress QPS observed: peak 912 qps
- Average effective batch size: 27.6 (baseline) vs 21.1 (tempering)
- KV hit-rate: 64% (baseline) vs 78% (tempering)
- p99: 238ms (baseline) vs 102ms (tempering)
- tokens/s: 41.9k (baseline) vs 39.2k (tempering)

Unresolved questions:
- Long-term: does tempering cause hidden fairness issues across tenants (priority inversion) — need per-tenant isolation tests.
- Cost model: quantify cost-per-millisecond saved in tail vs extra token cost from slightly reduced batching efficiency.

End-of-note.
